content: At birth, umbilical cord infections were historically a significant cause of neonatal mortality before the implementation of aseptic techniques. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of applying topical treatments to the umbilical cord in preventing infections, illnesses, and deaths in newborns. To conduct this analysis, researchers searched the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group trials register (as of September 2003) and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Issue 2, 2003). Additionally, they consulted experts in the field. The study included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared the use of topical cord care with no treatment, as well as comparisons between different types of cord care. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted relevant data. A total of 21 studies, involving 8,959 participants, were included in the review. Most of these studies were conducted in high-income countries. Importantly, none of the studies reported systemic infections or deaths among the participants. The findings revealed no significant difference in outcomes between umbilical cords treated with antiseptics and those managed with dry cord care or placebo. However, there was a trend suggesting reduced bacterial colonization when antibiotics were used compared to antiseptics or no treatment. It was also observed that the use of antiseptics delayed the time it took for the umbilical cord to naturally separate. Additionally, the application of antiseptics appeared to reduce maternal concerns regarding the condition of the umbilical cord. The authors concluded that there is a need for high-quality trials in low-income settings to better understand the impact of topical cord care in such environments. In high-income settings, the available research is limited and has not demonstrated a clear benefit of using antibiotics or antiseptics over simply keeping the umbilical cord clean. The overall quality of evidence supporting these findings is considered low.
